content: Sentinel site surveillance for Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) has been implemented in eight countries, starting in Bangladesh in 2012, followed by Indonesia and Nepal in 2014, Maldives in 2015, and Bhutan, India, Myanmar, and Timor-Leste in 2016. In Bangladesh, population-based CRS surveillance is also conducted, where all vaccine-preventable disease reporting sites include CRS case reporting. CRS is associated with significant morbidity and mortality, with an estimated mortality rate ranging from 20% to 40%. Infants born with cardiac defects are at the highest risk of mortality. Since 2010, the estimated mean incidence rate of CRS in the region has been 121 per 100,000 live births (95% CI: 31–238), with an annual total of 49,229 cases (95% CI: 11,204–96,976). The regional goal is to achieve measles and rubella elimination by 2023. The elimination of rubella in two countries within the region is estimated to have prevented 52,118 CRS cases annually. In 2020, Maldives and Sri Lanka were verified to have eliminated rubella, and both countries maintained their rubella-free status in 2021. Facility-based CRS surveillance in India revealed that approximately one-fifth of suspected CRS patients from 2016 to 2018 had laboratory-confirmed rubella infection, indicating ongoing rubella transmission in the country. The estimated CRS incidence in India varies depending on the model used, with one model estimating 6 cases per 100,000 live births, translating to approximately 14,520–50,028 infants with CRS annually. The rubella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine that provides more than 95% long-lasting immunity with a single dose, likely offering lifelong protection. Rubella vaccines are available as monovalent formulations or in combination with other vaccines, such as measles (MR), measles and mumps (MMR), or measles, mumps, and varicella (MMRV). To establish a CRS surveillance system, it is essential to have two national coordinators: one for epidemiology and one for laboratories. The epidemiological coordinator is responsible for developing protocols, training materials, and conducting training, monitoring surveillance performance, ensuring specimen collection and transport, maintaining the CRS database, coordinating with laboratories, and providing feedback to healthcare providers and public health authorities. The laboratory coordinator ensures adequate laboratory testing, quality assurance, interpretation of test results, and coordination with epidemiological activities. Healthcare facilities included in CRS surveillance should be those likely to encounter infants with common CRS-associated defects, such as cataracts, heart defects, or deafness, as well as those with a maternal history of rubella during pregnancy. Secondary and tertiary care facilities, such as children’s hospitals and centers for hearing and blindness, are ideal for sentinel surveillance. Local surveillance coordinators at sentinel sites ensure adherence to national protocols, assist in training healthcare providers, collect clinical and epidemiological data, ensure proper specimen collection and transport, maintain a line list of suspected CRS cases, and provide feedback to healthcare providers. Initial and refresher training for participating providers should be conducted annually, covering clinical features of CRS, evaluation of suspected cases, laboratory testing, case follow-up, infection control measures, and timely reporting. Surveillance quality assessments should be conducted at least every six months to evaluate the completeness of CRS surveillance. Missed cases can be identified by reviewing hospital records and comparing reported cases with suspected cases that meet inclusion criteria. The proportion of missed cases and untested reported cases should be assessed, and incomplete records should be addressed with site providers to emphasize the importance of data completeness. CRS surveillance data should be analyzed annually or more frequently if necessary, focusing on case classification, geographic distribution, clustering, maternal characteristics, and maternal exposure to rubella. Efforts should be made to expand CRS surveillance to include additional sites, especially in countries where pilot testing has been limited or where the current system does not capture the majority of suspected CRS cases. Feedback should be provided to stakeholders, including updates on CRS epidemiology and recommendations for improvement. Infection control measures are critical for infants with CRS, as they may shed the rubella virus for up to one year and can cause outbreaks. Only individuals immune to rubella should have contact with affected infants. In hospitals, affected infants should be placed in contact isolation, and caregivers should wear protective gowns and gloves and be immunized against rubella. Specimen collection for CRS surveillance involves obtaining biological samples for virus detection/isolation and antibody level detection. Nasopharyngeal swabs are preferred for virus isolation, but other acceptable specimens include throat swabs, nasal swabs, blood, urine, cerebrospinal fluid, and dried blood spots. Proper storage and transport conditions, such as refrigeration or freezing at -70°C, are essential to preserve sample integrity.
